question: Which of the following is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to performing a lumbar puncture?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While thrombocytopenia increases bleeding risk and requires caution, a platelet count of 60 × 10⁹/L is not the absolute contraindication to LP. The usual threshold varies (often <50 × 10⁹/L is relative contraindication), but clinical urgency can override this.

answers.text: Presence of papilloedema on fundoscopy suggesting raised ICP

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Papilloedema indicating raised intracranial pressure is an absolute contraindication to LP without prior neuroimaging. Performing LP in the presence of raised ICP risks tonsillar herniation ('coning') — a fatal complication. Urgent CT must precede LP in this scenario.

Incorrect. Anticoagulation at therapeutic levels is a relative contraindication requiring warfarin reversal before LP, but it is not absolute. Clinical urgency (e.g., suspected bacterial meningitis) may mandate proceeding after risk-benefit assessment.

Incorrect. Local skin infection at the intended puncture site is a contraindication at that site, but LP can proceed at a different uninfected interspace. It is not an absolute contraindication to LP altogether.

overallFeedback.feedback: The absolute contraindication to LP is clinical or fundoscopic evidence of raised intracranial pressure (papilloedema, midline shift on CT). LP without prior imaging in raised ICP risks fatal herniation.
Correct. Papilloedema indicating raised ICP is an absolute contraindication to LP without prior CT imaging — due to the risk of fatal brainstem herniation.
